# Operational Monitoring and Error Detection for Electromagnetic Actuators

### System Overview
An electromagnetic actuator serves as a primary electromechanical transducer, converting electrical energy into mechanical energy to control fluid or gas flow. The actuator operates using an electric coil wound around a magnetic core. When energized, the coil generates a magnetic field that acts upon a movable valve body, driving it into a desired position to open, close, or regulate a passage.

### Current Monitoring and Data Collection
To ensure precise operation and monitor the physical health of the actuator, an integrated control unit (controller) continuously monitors the system. During operation, the controller measures the profile of the electrical current flowing through the coil. Because the movement of the valve body and the changing magnetic flux induce back-electromotive force (back-EMF), variations in the current curve directly correspond to the mechanical movement and state of the actuator.

### Parameter Extraction and Evaluation Product
From the monitored current curve, the controller identifies and isolates a specific temporal evaluation section. This time window is defined by three key parameters:
1. **Starting Current Value ($I_{\text{start}}$):** The electrical current measured at the beginning of the evaluation window.
2. **Ending Current Value ($I_{\text{end}}$):** The electrical current measured at the conclusion of the evaluation window.
3. **Duration Period ($\Delta t$):** The total elapsed time between the start and end points of the evaluation section.

Using these three parameters, the controller processes the isolated data to compute a characteristic **evaluation product**. This product mathematically combines the dynamic electrical behavior ($I_{\text{start}}$ and $I_{\text{end}}$) with the temporal behavior ($\Delta t$) of the actuation cycle.

### Diagnostic Thresholding and Fault Detection
Finally, the system uses the calculated evaluation product to perform real-time diagnostics. The controller compares the calculated value against a set of predefined operational limits or thresholds stored in its memory. 

If the evaluation product falls outside the acceptable range, the controller identifies an error function within the actuator. This diagnostic capability allows the system to detect operational anomalies—such as mechanical sticking, increased friction, coil degradation, or abnormal supply voltage—before total component failure occurs, enabling safe operation and timely maintenance.

# Technical Specification & Method Description
**Document Title:** Real-Time Monitoring and Diagnostic Method for Electromagnetic Valve Actuators  
**Field of Invention:** Automotive & Industrial Fluid Control Systems / Embedded Diagnostics  

---

## 1. System Overview and Context

Electromagnetic actuators—commonly referred to as solenoids—are vital components in modern fluid control systems, including fuel injection systems, automatic transmissions, braking modules, and industrial pneumatic lines. These actuators rely on an energizing current passing through an internal electric coil to generate a magnetic field. This field exerts force on a moveable armature, displacing a valve element to open, close, or modulate fluid flow.

Because mechanical failure, mechanical wear, fluid contamination, or electrical degradation can cause catastrophic system failures, continuous operational monitoring is required. Traditional diagnostic methods often require additional physical sensors (such as optical or magnetic position sensors) to verify mechanical movement. These extra components increase system complexity, cost, and potential points of failure. 

This document describes a non-invasive, sensor-less monitoring method executed directly by an electronic control unit (ECU). The method evaluates the dynamic current profile passing through the actuator's coil during a defined time window to reliably detect operational errors.

---

## 2. Hardware Architecture

The system consists of the following primary sub-components:

1. **Electromagnetic Actuator:** Comprises a stator coil, a return spring, and a moving armature connected to a valve head.
2. **Current Sensing Circuitry:** A low-side shunt resistor or inline Hall-effect sensor integrated into the coil driver circuit, capable of real-time current sampling.
3. **Controller / Microcontroller:** An embedded processor equipped with an Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC), a precise hardware timer, memory (ROM/RAM for storing thresholds), and diagnostic execution logic.

```
+------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                            CONTROLLER                            |
|  +--------------------+   +-------------------+   +-----------+  |
|  |  Driver Circuit    |   | Diagnostic Engine |   | Threshold |  |
|  |  (PWM / Switch)    |   | (Eval Product)    |   |  Storage  |  |
|  +---------+----------+   +---------^---------+   +-----+-----+  |
+------------|------------------------|-------------------|--------+
             |                        |                   |
             v                        |                   v
     +---------------+        +-------+-------+    +--------------+
     | Electric Coil | ------ | Current Sense |    | System Fault |
     |  (Actuator)   |        |  (Shunt/ADC)  |    |     Flag     |
     +-------+-------+        +---------------+    +--------------+
             |
             v
     +---------------+
     | Armature/Valve|
     +---------------+
```

---

## 3. Physical Principle of Operation

When voltage is applied to the actuator coil, current begins to rise exponentially according to the coil's electrical time constant ($\tau = L/R$). As the magnetic force overcomes the mechanical resistance and spring pre-load, the armature begins to move. 

The physical movement of the armature inside the magnetic circuit alters the magnetic inductance ($L$) over time and induces a counter-electromotive force (back-EMF). This movement creates a characteristic dynamic dip or plateau in the current response curve. By analyzing this specific section of the current curve, the controller can infer mechanical movement, travel speed, and overall actuator health without external position sensors.

---

## 4. Method of Monitoring and Error Detection

The control unit executes a four-step diagnostic procedure during every actuation cycle (or at predetermined monitoring intervals):

```
       Current (I)
         ^
         |                    I_end  *
         |                          /
         |                         /
         |                        /  <-- Temporal Section
         |              I_start  *
         |                     /
         |       Back-EMF     /
         |       Inductance  /
         |         Dip      /
         |        _        /
         |       / \______/
         +------------------------------------> Time (t)
                         |<------ Delta t ------>|
                         t1                     t2
```

### Step 1: Definition of the Temporal Section
The controller establishes a specific **Temporal Section** $[t_1, t_2]$ within the actuation period. This section is chosen specifically to encompass the phase where mechanical displacement occurs or where the current profile is most sensitive to variations in magnetic resistance and mechanical friction.

### Step 2: Measurement of Dynamic Parameters
During the designated temporal section, the controller samples the current via the ADC and records three specific variables:
1. **Starting Current ($I_{start}$):** The measured electrical current at time $t_1$.
2. **Ending Current ($I_{end}$):** The measured electrical current at time $t_2$.
3. **Duration ($\Delta t$):** The precise elapsed time of the section ($\Delta t = t_2 - t_1$).

### Step 3: Calculation of the Evaluation Product
Using the captured variables, the controller calculates a dimensionless or scaled numerical metric termed the **Evaluation Product ($P_{eval}$)**. Depending on the preferred calibration model, the evaluation product reflects the current gradient, effective energy rate, or profile area.

A primary formulation for the Evaluation Product is defined as:

$$P_{eval} = \frac{I_{end} - I_{start}}{\Delta t}$$

*Alternative formulations may weight the duration or delta-current non-linearly to emphasize small changes in valve response:*

$$P_{eval} = (I_{end} - I_{start}) \cdot f(\Delta t)$$

### Step 4: Threshold Comparison and Diagnostic Output
The calculated $P_{eval}$ is compared against predefined, pre-calibrated upper and lower limit thresholds stored in the controller's memory:

*   **$P_{min}$:** Minimum allowable limit (indicating sluggish movement or excessive friction).
*   **$P_{max}$:** Maximum allowable limit (indicating mechanical blockage, missing armature load, or electrical shorting).

$$\text{Status} = 
\begin{cases} 
\text{NORMAL} & \text{if } P_{min} \le P_{eval} \le P_{max} \\
\text{FAULT DETECTED} & \text{if } P_{eval} < P_{min} \text{ or } P_{eval} > P_{max}
\end{cases}$$

---

## 5. Detected Fault Conditions

This evaluation methodology allows the controller to reliably identify several distinct error modes:

| Fault Condition | Cause / Mechanism | Impact on $P_{eval}$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Mechanical Sticking / Sluggishness** | Debris, varnish, or high fluid viscosity slows down armature movement. | $\Delta t$ effectively expands or $I_{end}$ lags, causing $P_{eval}$ to drop below $P_{min}$. |
| **Complete Valve Seizure** | Armature is mechanically locked; no movement occurs, generating no back-EMF. | Current rises purely exponentially; $I_{end} - I_{start}$ is abnormally high, pushing $P_{eval}$ above $P_{max}$. |
| **Broken Return Spring** | Reduced mechanical resistance allows hyper-fast movement. | Uncharacteristic current transient alters the shape, causing $P_{eval}$ to breach calibration limits. |
| **Electrical Coil Degradation** | Partial shorting of coil windings reduces inductance. | Current rises too rapidly; $I_{end}$ reaches threshold prematurely, triggering an out-of-bounds $P_{eval}$. |

---

## 6. Key Advantages

1. **Cost and Space Savings:** Eliminates the need for discrete position, displacement, or pressure sensors at the valve site.
2. **High Reliability:** Operates entirely digitally within the controller, making it immune to environmental degradation typical of external physical sensors (such as thermal degradation, fluid exposure, or mechanical vibration).
3. **Real-time Diagnostic Capability:** Detects operational drift *before* full functional failure occurs, enabling predictive maintenance and safe-state fail-over protocols in critical control systems.

**The Heart of Electromagnetism: Understanding the Magnetic Core**

In the modern world, electricity powers almost every aspect of our daily lives, from the smartphone in your pocket to the massive power grids illuminating entire cities. Yet, behind the scenes of these incredible technological achievements lies an unsung hero: **a magnetic core**. 

Though often hidden deep within electronic components, a magnetic core is fundamental to the operation of transformers, electric motors, generators, and inductors. But what exactly is a magnetic core, and why is it so vital to modern technology?

---

### What is a Magnetic Core?

At its simplest, a magnetic core is a piece of magnetic material—usually iron, steel, or ferrite—around which wire coils are wound. Its primary job is to confine and guide magnetic fields created by electric currents. 

While magnetic fields can travel through the air, air is a relatively poor conductor of magnetism. A magnetic core acts like a "superhighway" for magnetic flux. Because the core has high **magnetic permeability** (meaning it easily accepts a magnetic field), it concentrates the magnetic force, making the component exponentially more efficient and powerful than if it relied on air alone.

---

### How It Works

When an electric current flows through a wire wrapped around a core, it creates a magnetic field. The domains within the magnetic core align with this field, vastly increasing its strength. 

* In a **transformer**, a magnetic core transfers electrical energy from one coil of wire to another through electromagnetic induction, allowing voltage to be stepped up (increased) for long-distance power transmission, or stepped down (decreased) for safe household use.
* In an **electric motor**, the interaction between the core’s magnetic field and the electric current generates the physical force needed to spin a rotor.

---

### Common Materials Used for Magnetic Cores

Different applications require different core materials, depending on the frequency and power of the electrical current:

1. **Solid and Laminated Iron/Silicon Steel:** Used in low-frequency applications like standard AC power transformers. Cores are often "laminated"—built from thin, insulated sheets of steel stacked together—to reduce energy loss.
2. **Ferrite Cores:** Made from ceramic compounds containing iron oxide mixed with metals like nickel or zinc. Ferrites do not conduct electricity well, making them ideal for high-frequency applications, such as computer power supplies, radios, and telecommunications.
3. **Powdered Metal Cores:** Made of fine metal powders bound together. These are excellent for applications requiring high magnetic stability and high energy storage.

---

### Overcoming Energy Losses

Designing an effective magnetic core is a constant battle against energy efficiency loss. Engineers primarily design cores to minimize two main phenomena:

* **Hysteresis Loss:** As alternating current (AC) continually shifts direction, the internal magnetic domains of the core must constantly flip. This friction-like process generates heat, wasting energy.
* **Eddy Currents:** The changing magnetic field induces small, swirling electrical currents within the core material itself. These "eddy currents" generate unwanted heat. Using laminated sheets or non-conductive ferrite materials helps break up these currents and keep the system cool and efficient.

---

### Conclusion

Without the magnetic core, the electrical devices we rely on today would be drastically larger, vastly less efficient, and far more expensive. By channeling the invisible force of magnetism with incredible precision, the magnetic core remains one of the foundational building blocks of electrical engineering—silently driving the technology that keeps the modern world running.

# Technical Specification: Electronic Controller Diagnostic Engine for Electromagnetic Valve Actuators

**Document Identifier:** TS-EVA-202309-DEP  
**Revision:** 2.1  
**Classification:** Engineering Technical Standard  
**Subject:** Diagnostic Evaluation Product (DEP) Calculation via Actuation Current Profile Parameters  

---

## 1. System Overview & Scope

This specification defines the functional, mathematical, and algorithmic requirements for an Electronic Control Unit (ECU) monitoring an electromagnetic valve actuator system. 

The system evaluates actuator health and mechanical response during each stroke event. By capturing discrete current state points—Start Current ($I_{\text{start}}$), End Current ($I_{\text{end}}$)—and the Actuation Duration ($t_{\text{act}}$), the controller calculates a dimensionless or standardized metric termed the **Diagnostic Evaluation Product (DEP)**. 

```
          Current (I)
             ^
   I_end ----|-------------------------+  <- Sampled at t_end
             |                        /|
             |                       / |
             |                      /  |
             |                     /   |
   I_start --|----x               /    |  <- Sampled at t_start
             |    |              /     |
             +----+-------------+------+--> Time (t)
               t_start        t_act   t_end
```

---

## 2. Parameter Definitions & Signal Measurement

### 2.1 Input Signals

| Parameter | Symbol | Unit | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Start Current** | $I_{\text{start}}$ | Amperes ($A$) | Measured current sampled at the onset of the mechanical displacement phase ($t_0$). |
| **End Current** | $I_{\text{end}}$ | Amperes ($A$) | Measured current sampled at the end of the pull-in phase or driver pulse boundary ($t_{\text{end}}$). |
| **Actuation Duration** | $t_{\text{act}}$ | Milliseconds ($ms$) | Total elapsed time from actuation trigger ($t_0$) to command termination or holding state transition ($t_{\text{end}}$). |

### 2.2 Signal Acquisition Requirements

1. **Current Sensing:** Measured via a low-inductance shunt resistor and a differential operational amplifier, sampled by an internal 12-bit Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) at a minimum frequency $f_s \ge 20\text{ kHz}$.
2. **Timing Accuracy:** $t_{\text{act}}$ shall be captured using a hardware timer module with a time-base resolution of $\le 1\,\mu\text{s}$.

---

## 3. Mathematical Model of the Diagnostic Evaluation Product (DEP)

The Diagnostic Evaluation Product (DEP) quantifies the electromechanical energy state and mechanical impedance of the solenoid stroke. It is calculated as a composite function combining the integrated charge proxy ($\mathcal{Q}$) and the dynamic current gradient ($\mathcal{G}$).

### 3.1 Primary Component Functions

#### 3.1.1 Mean Charge Factor ($\mathcal{Q}$)
Assuming a trapezoidal integration over the defined window $[t_{\text{start}}, t_{\text{end}}]$, the charge factor represents the total energy delivered to overcome counter-forces (magnetic gap flux build-up and mechanical spring return):

$$\mathcal{Q} = \left( \frac{I_{\text{start}} + I_{\text{end}}}{2} \right) \cdot t_{\text{act}}$$

#### 3.1.2 Dynamic Gradient Factor ($\mathcal{G}$)
The dynamic gradient assesses changes in coil inductance caused by the movement of the ferromagnetic core (armature displacement inflection):

$$\mathcal{G} = \frac{I_{\text{end}} - I_{\text{start}}}{t_{\text{act}} + \epsilon}$$

*Note: $\epsilon = 10^{-6}\text{ ms}$ is a non-zero computational constant added to prevent division-by-zero errors.*

---

### 3.2 Standard DEP Equation

The controller executes the DEP calculation using the following unified formula:

$$\text{DEP} = k_{\text{cal}} \cdot \left[ \left( \frac{I_{\text{start}} + I_{\text{end}}}{2} \right) \cdot t_{\text{act}} \right] \cdot \left[ 1 + \alpha \cdot \left( \frac{I_{\text{end}} - I_{\text{start}}}{t_{\text{act}} + \epsilon} \right) \right]$$

Where:
* $k_{\text{cal}}$ is a system calibration scalar (typically $1.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ A}^{-1}\text{ms}^{-1}$).
* $\alpha$ is a dynamic weight coefficient determined during end-of-line (EOL) calibration.

---

## 4. Controller Algorithm Execution Logic

The controller shall execute the evaluation pipeline according to the state machine logic below:

```
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                       STATE 0: IDLE / WAITING                         |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                   |
                   Command Received (Trigger = TRUE)
                                   v
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                       STATE 1: ACQUISITION                            |
| 1. Capture I_start at t_0                                             |
| 2. Start hardware timer for t_act                                     |
| 3. Continuous ADC buffer filling                                      |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                   |
                 Actuation Window Complete (Command = OFF)
                                   v
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                       STATE 2: FEATURE EXTRACTION                     |
| 1. Stop timer; register t_act = t_end - t_0                           |
| 2. Capture I_end from ADC buffer                                      |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                   |
                                   v
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                       STATE 3: MATHEMATICAL COMPUTATION               |
| 1. Q_raw = 0.5 * (I_start + I_end) * t_act                            |
| 2. G_raw = (I_end - I_start) / (t_act + EPSILON)                      |
| 3. DEP = k_cal * Q_raw * (1 + alpha * G_raw)                          |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                   |
                                   v
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                       STATE 4: FAULT CLASSIFICATION                   |
| Evaluate DEP against pre-set threshold limits: [DEP_MIN, DEP_MAX]     |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

---

## 5. Diagnostic Fault Classification Matrix

The computed DEP value is mapped to health states stored in non-volatile memory (EEPROM/Flash).

$$\text{Health Status} = 
\begin{cases} 
\text{PASS (Normal Operation)}, & \text{DEP}_{\text{low\_warn}} \le \text{DEP} \le \text{DEP}_{\text{high\_warn}} \\
\text{FAULT: Mechanical Stiction / Slow Response}, & \text{DEP} > \text{DEP}_{\text{high\_crit}} \\
\text{FAULT: Coil Degradation / Turn Short}, & \text{DEP} < \text{DEP}_{\text{low\_crit}} \quad \text{AND} \quad \mathcal{G} > \mathcal{G}_{\text{threshold}} \\
\text{FAULT: Valve Jam / Blocked Armature}, & \text{DEP} < \text{DEP}_{\text{low\_crit}} \quad \text{AND} \quad \mathcal{G} \approx 0
\end{cases}$$

### Detailed Fault Mapping Table

| Metric Deviation | Root Cause Mechanism | System Action / Diagnostic Trouble Code (DTC) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **$\text{DEP} > \text{DEP}_{\text{high\_crit}}$** | Excessive $t_{\text{act}}$ due to mechanical drag, increased fluid viscosity, or weak return spring. | Flag DTC `P09A1` (Actuator Slow Response); Switch to limpmode / duty cycle reduction. |
| **$\text{DEP} < \text{DEP}_{\text{low\_crit}}$ (Low $t_{\text{act}}$)** | Shortened stroke due to mechanical obstruction preventing full armature movement. | Flag DTC `P09A2` (Actuator Stroke Incomplete); Disable high-side driver. |
| **High $\mathcal{G}$, Low DEP** | Winding insulation breakdown causing lower inductance ($L$), leading to an unusually fast current ramp ($I_{\text{end}} \gg I_{\text{start}}$ in minimal time). | Flag DTC `P09A3` (Actuator Electrical Overcurrent / Short-Turn); Open safety relay. |

---

## 6. Execution Constraints & Operational Requirements

### 6.1 Real-Time Performance
* The calculation phase (State 3) must complete within **$\le 500\,\mu\text{s}$** following the termination of $t_{\text{act}}$.
* Floating-point arithmetic operations must execute using the MCU’s hardware Floating-Point Unit (FPU) or an optimized fixed-point bit-shift arithmetic library.

### 6.2 Temperature Compensation
Because copper coil resistance ($R_{\text{coil}}$) changes with temperature, $I_{\text{start}}$ and $I_{\text{end}}$ drift across thermal ranges. The controller must scale raw DEP results using a measured coil temperature ($T_{\text{coil}}$):

$$\text{DEP}_{\text{compensated}} = \frac{\text{DEP}_{\text{raw}}}{1 + \beta_{\text{Cu}} (T_{\text{coil}} - 20^\circ\text{C})}$$

Where $\beta_{\text{Cu}} = 0.00393 \text{ K}^{-1}$ (Temperature coefficient of copper).

---

## 7. Verification & Acceptance Criteria

1. **Precision:** Computed DEP must demonstrate a coefficient of variation ($CV$) $< 1.5\%$ across 1,000 baseline cycles under identical hydraulic and thermal conditions.
2. **Fault Detection Sensitivity:** The algorithm must detect an artificial insertion of mechanical resistance resulting in a $\ge 10\%$ increase in $t_{\text{act}}$ within **a single actuation cycle**.

### Option 1: System Claim (Apparatus)

**1. A system for detecting fault conditions in an electromagnetically actuated valve, the system comprising:**
* an electromagnetic actuator comprising a coil and a magnetic core configured to translate and drive a valve member; and
* a controller operatively coupled to the coil, the controller configured to:
  * measure a current passing through the coil;
  * select a time interval having a defined duration;
  * sample a first current value at a start of the time interval and a second current value at an end of the time interval;
  * calculate an evaluation product as a function of the first current value, the second current value, and the duration of the time interval;
  * compare the evaluation product to a predetermined threshold value; and
  * indicate a fault condition of the valve when the evaluation product exceeds the predetermined threshold value.

---

### Option 2: Method Claim (Process)

**2. A method for monitoring operation of a valve driven by an electromagnetic actuator having an electric coil and a magnetic core, the method comprising:**
* measuring, by a control circuit, an electrical current flowing through the electric coil;
* selecting a time interval characterized by a start time, an end time, and a duration;
* determining an initial current value at the start time and a final current value at the end time;
* generating an evaluation product comprising a mathematical product derived from the initial current value, the final current value, and the duration;
* comparing the evaluation product against a threshold limit; and
* outputting a fault signal upon determining that the evaluation product exceeds the threshold limit.

---

### Option 3: Dependent Claims (For adding specific scope)

* **3. The system of claim 1,** wherein the evaluation product is calculated by multiplying a difference between the second current value and the first current value by the duration.
* **4. The system of claim 1,** wherein the controller is further configured to de-energize the coil in response to indicating the fault condition.

---

### Key Legal/Technical Terminology Used:
* **"Operatively coupled / Operatively connected":** Standard broad patent language to indicate parts work together without dictating exact physical mounting.
* **"Translate and drive":** Broad legal descriptions of movement rather than just "moves."
* **"Evaluation product":** Captures the mathematical result of multiplication while allowing flexibility in how the variables are combined.
* **"Predetermined threshold value / Threshold limit":** Broad terms for "limit."
* **"Fault condition":** Legally broader than "fault function" or "malfunction."

counterfactuals.output:
Here is a snippet formatted in standard patent specification style (including Field of Invention, Abstract, Detailed Description excerpt, and Claims) for an apparatus that detects operational errors in a solenoid/electromagnetic valve.

***

**UNITED STATES PATENT APPLICATION**

**TITLE:** APPARATUS AND SYSTEM FOR REAL-TIME ERROR FUNCTION DETECTION IN AN ELECTROMAGNETIC COIL-DRIVEN VALVE

---

### ABSTRACT
An diagnostic apparatus for detecting operational error functions in an electromagnetic coil-driven valve includes a current sensing circuit operably coupled to the electromagnetic coil, a voltage sensor, and a processing unit. The processing unit is configured to capture a dynamic current response profile of the coil during an activation event. By analyzing transient features of the current response profile—specifically identifying the presence, magnitude, and timing of a inflection point corresponding to mechanical armature movement—the processing unit compares the captured profile against a set of predetermined healthy valve signatures. Deviations indicate specific error functions, including mechanical sticking, coil short-circuiting, thermal degradation, or partial armature obstruction, allowing real-time fault reporting.

---

### DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF PREFERRED EMBODIMENTS (EXCERPT)

Referring to **FIG. 1**, the diagnostic apparatus **100** is integrated with an electromagnetic coil-driven valve **102**. The valve **102** comprises an electromagnetic coil **104**, a stationary core, and a movable armature **106** biased by a return spring **108**. 

When a drive voltage is applied by the valve driver **110**, current begins to ramp up through the coil **104**. As the magnetic field builds, the armature **106** moves from a first position to a second position. This mechanical motion changes the magnetic reluctance of the magnetic circuit, inducing a back-electromotive force (back-EMF) that causes a characteristic dip or inflection point in the rising current waveform (hereinafter referred to as the "inflection point").

```
Current (I)
  ^
  |        /-- Peak Current
  |       / 
  |      /  <-- Inflection Point (Armature Movement)
  |  /\ /
  | /  V
  |/___________________> Time (t)
```

The apparatus **100** includes a high-side or low-side current sense resistor **112** (or alternatively, a Hall-effect sensor) electrically connected in series with the coil **104**. A high-speed Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) **114** samples the voltage drop across the current sense resistor **112** at a predetermined sampling rate (e.g., 100 kHz) during the valve actuation window.

A digital signal processor (DSP) or microcontroller **116** receives the sampled current data and executes an error detection algorithm. The algorithm calculates the first derivative ($dI/dt$) and second derivative ($d^2I/dt^2$) of the current waveform to precisely detect the timing ($t_{inflect}$) and current level ($I_{inflect}$) of the inflection point.

The microcontroller **116** evaluates error functions according to the following criteria:
1. **Mechanical Sticking/Jamming:** If $dI/dt$ remains strictly positive without a local minimum or downward inflection within a maximum expected time window ($t_{max}$), the apparatus outputs an "Armature Stuck Closed" fault code.
2. **Slow Response / Mechanical Degradation:** If the inflection point $t_{inflect}$ occurs later than a upper threshold ($t_{threshold\_high}$), the apparatus identifies increased mechanical friction, fluid contamination, or degraded spring tension.
3. **Turn-to-Turn Coil Short:** If the initial slope of the current ramp ($dI/dt_{initial}$) exceeds a short-circuit threshold prior to armature movement, indicating reduced coil inductance, an "Electrical Fault - Short Circuit" signal is latched, and driver **110** is immediately disabled to prevent thermal runaway.

---

### WE CLAIM:

**1. An apparatus for detecting operational error functions in an electromagnetic coil-driven valve, the apparatus comprising:**
*   a current sensing circuit configured to measure an electrical current passing through an electromagnetic coil of the valve during an activation cycle;
*   a timing module; and
*   a processing unit communicably coupled to the current sensing circuit and the timing module, the processing unit configured to:
    *   sample a dynamic current profile of the coil during the activation cycle;
    *   detect a local inflection point in the dynamic current profile caused by back-electromotive force generated by movement of a valve armature;
    *   extract at least one temporal parameter and at least one magnitude parameter associated with the local inflection point;
    *   compare the extracted parameters against a stored reference matrix; and
    *   generate an error signal responsive to the extracted parameters failing to satisfy a target criteria defined by the reference matrix.

**2. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the generated error signal indicates a mechanical sticking fault of the armature when the processing unit fails to detect the local inflection point within a predefined actuation time window.**

**3. The apparatus of claim 1, further comprising a temperature sensor configured to measure an ambient or coil temperature, wherein the processing unit dynamically adjusts the stored reference matrix based on the measured temperature to compensate for temperature-induced coil resistance changes.**

**4. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the processing unit is further configured to compute a first derivative ($dI/dt$) of the sampled current profile, wherein the local inflection point is identified by a zero-crossing of the first derivative.**

counterfactuals.prompt: How can a controller monitor current in an electromagnetic actuator to detect mechanical or electrical faults using a threshold comparison method? Write out the system description in claim format.
counterfactuals.output:
### Overview of the Fault Detection Method

When a controller energizes an electromagnetic actuator (such as a solenoid, relay, or motor), the resulting current waveform provides direct insight into both the electrical circuit and the physical motion of the actuator.

1. **Electrical Faults:**
   * **Short Circuit:** Results in an extremely fast current rise rate ($di/dt$) and a steady-state current exceeding the upper threshold limit.
   * **Open Circuit / High Resistance:** Results in zero current or a current rise that fails to reach the lower activation threshold limit within a specified time window.

2. **Mechanical Faults:**
   * **Mechanical Jam / Stiction:** Under normal operation, as the movable armature moves through the magnetic field, it generates a back-electromotive force (back-EMF). This causes a characteristic "dip" or plateau in the rising current waveform (the motion dip). If the armature is jammed, no back-EMF is produced, and the current rises monotonically to a higher level without the characteristic dip.
   * **Increased Friction / Binding:** Delays the onset of movement, causing the current dip to occur outside expected lower/upper time boundaries.

By comparing the measured current against **static thresholds** (absolute min/max current) and **dynamic/time-windowed thresholds** (sampling at specific time intervals $t_1, t_2$), the controller can isolate specific mechanical and electrical faults.

---

### System Description in Claim Format

**1. A fault detection system for an electromagnetic actuator, the system comprising:**

*   an **electromagnetic actuator** comprising at least one inductive coil and a movable mechanical element arranged to move in response to an energized state of the inductive coil;
*   a **drive circuit** configured to selectively supply an electrical drive signal to the inductive coil;
*   a **current sensor** electrically coupled to the inductive coil and configured to measure an operating current flowing through the inductive coil and output a representative current signal; and
*   a **controller** comprising a processor and a memory storing executable instructions and a set of predefined threshold parameters, wherein the controller is operatively connected to the current sensor and the drive circuit, the controller configured to:
    *   receive the current signal from the current sensor during actuation of the electromagnetic actuator;
    *   sample the current signal over a predefined time interval to generate an observed current profile;
    *   compare at least one feature of the observed current profile against the set of predefined threshold parameters;
    *   determine the presence of a fault condition based on said comparison; and
    *   execute a responsive action upon determining the presence of the fault condition, wherein the fault condition comprises at least one of an electrical fault and a mechanical fault.

---

**2. The system of claim 1, wherein the set of predefined threshold parameters comprises an upper magnitude threshold and a lower magnitude threshold, and wherein the controller is configured to detect an electrical short-circuit fault when the observed current profile exceeds the upper magnitude threshold.**

---

**3. The system of claim 1, wherein the controller is configured to detect an open-circuit fault or supply interruption when the observed current profile fails to reach a minimum lower magnitude threshold within a first designated time window following initiation of the drive signal.**

---

**4. The system of claim 1, wherein the observed current profile includes a local current minimum corresponding to a back-electromotive force (back-EMF) induced by movement of the movable mechanical element, and wherein the set of predefined threshold parameters comprises:**
*   a upper time threshold boundary; and
*   a lower time threshold boundary defining an expected motion time window;

*wherein the controller is configured to detect a mechanical fault when the local current minimum occurs outside of the expected motion time window or is absent from the observed current profile.*

---

**5. The system of claim 4, wherein the mechanical fault identified by the controller is a jammed mechanical element condition characterized by the complete absence of the local current minimum due to the lack of movement-induced back-EMF.**

---

**6. The system of claim 1, wherein the controller is configured to evaluate a rate of change of current ($di/dt$) within the observed current profile against a predefined slope threshold parameter, wherein a rate of change exceeding the slope threshold parameter indicates an electrical short between coil turns, and a rate of change below the slope threshold parameter indicates mechanical binding or excessive friction.**

---

**7. The system of claim 1, wherein the responsive action executed by the controller comprises at least one of:**
*   de-energizing the drive circuit to prevent thermal damage to the coil;
*   setting a diagnostic fault flag in the memory; and
*   transmitting a fault signal to an external system monitoring network.
